opus-5.5.text:
I think scaling has been genuinely surprising, and I don't want to be one of those people who dismisses it, because the results are real. If you'd told me ten years ago that you could get this much competence out of predicting the next token on enough data with enough compute, I would have been skeptical. So credit where it's due.

But I think of scaling as a strategy that buys you a particular kind of intelligence, and it's worth being precise about what that is. What you get is something like a very powerful amortized inference machine. You've seen an enormous number of situations, and you've compressed them into a function that maps inputs to plausible outputs very quickly. That's incredibly useful. It's also, I'd argue, only one half of what intelligence is.

The other half is what happens when you encounter something that isn't well covered by your past experience. A scientist facing a new phenomenon, a child figuring out a new toy, anyone in a novel situation. What they do isn't just pattern-matching against stored experience. They build a model of the situation, often a causal one, they form hypotheses, they run little experiments, they revise. That's a process of inference and model construction that happens at test time, on the fly, and it's very sample-efficient. You don't need a billion examples of a new kind of machine to figure out how it works. You poke at it.

So my concern with scaling as *the* strategy is that it tends to conflate having seen a lot with being able to reason about what you haven't seen. And as you scale, it gets harder and harder to tell which one you're observing, because the training distribution swallows so much of the world. Benchmarks that looked like tests of reasoning turn out to be partially tests of coverage.

Now, the interesting development in the last couple of years is that the scaling community has itself moved toward test-time compute: search, reasoning traces, verification. I think that's an implicit acknowledgment of the point. Pure amortization runs out, and you need some process that actually deliberates about the specific problem in front of you. Where I'd push further is on the *structure* of that deliberation. I think it should look less like generating long chains of text and more like building and querying explicit models of the world: probabilistic, causal, with the ability to say "if I intervened here, what would happen?" That's the kind of thing probabilistic programming and causal modeling were designed for, and I think the right synthesis uses learned systems to make that kind of inference tractable, rather than replacing it.

So to summarize, I don't see scaling and structured reasoning as opposing camps. Scaling gives you incredibly good intuitions and priors. But intelligence, especially the kind we care about for science and discovery, requires being able to go beyond your priors in a principled way. And I don't think you get that for free just by making the prior bigger.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling provides only one half of intelligence and that going beyond prior experience does not come for free by making the prior bigger.

r002.rationale: It notes that the scaling community has moved toward test-time compute, but does not identify researchers’ pursuit of scaling as a pragmatic reason to pursue alternatives.

r003.rationale: It advocates using learned systems to make probabilistic and causal modeling tractable, combining scaled learning with structured reasoning methods.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I have a somewhat contrarian view on this, or at least a nuanced one. I don't think scaling is wrong, exactly. The results speak for themselves in a lot of ways. If you make the models bigger and you give them more data, they get better at a huge range of things, and I think anybody who denied that a few years ago has been proven pretty decisively wrong.

But I think there's a conflation happening between two different questions. One is, does scaling improve performance on the kinds of things these systems already do? And the answer there is clearly yes. The other is, does scaling get you to the thing we actually mean when we say intelligence? And there I'm much less sure, because I don't think the limitation is primarily one of capacity. I think it's one of what the systems are fundamentally doing.

The way I think about it, a lot of what we call intelligence is the ability to build models of the world, to form hypotheses about how things work, and then to reason with those models, to run them forward, to intervene on them, to ask what would happen if things were different. That's the inductive, model-building side. And then there's the deductive side, where you take the model you have and derive consequences that aren't obvious, that you've never seen before. Current systems are extraordinarily good at something that looks a bit like both of those, but which is really a very sophisticated form of interpolation over an enormous corpus of human behavior.

And the thing is, interpolation gets you remarkably far when the corpus is the entire internet. So you can mistake it for the real thing for a long time. But I think you see the cracks in exactly the places you'd predict. Problems that are genuinely novel, where there's no nearby example in the training distribution. Problems that require you to maintain a precise structured representation and reason over it for many steps without drift. Problems where the answer depends on a small number of hard constraints rather than on a large number of soft statistical cues. Those are the places where scaling helps less than you'd hope, and in some cases it barely helps at all.

So my view is that scaling is a necessary component but not a sufficient one. What's missing is something more like an architecture for learning programs, or learning models in the sense that a scientist means it, representations that have compositional structure, where you can combine pieces you've learned in new ways and get guaranteed behavior out of the combination. Humans do this. A child who learns what a wheel does and what a lever does can reason about a machine that combines them without having seen that machine. That's not interpolation. That's composition over a learned representation, and it's the thing I think we still don't really know how to get out of gradient descent on a big transformer.

The other thing I'd say is that the scaling strategy has a kind of built-in epistemic problem, which is that it's very hard to tell from the outside whether a capability came from genuine generalization or from the fact that something very similar was in the data. When the training set is unimaginably large, the counterfactual of what the model would do on a truly unseen problem becomes almost impossible to evaluate. So we end up with benchmarks that get saturated, and then we argue about whether that reflects progress or contamination, and I don't think either side can really settle it. That, to me, is a signal that we're measuring the wrong thing.

So if you ask me how I think about it as a strategy, I'd say scaling is the strategy that works right now, and it would be foolish to abandon it. But the question I'm more interested in is what you build on top of it, or alongside it, to get at the parts of intelligence that scaling seems to be asymptoting toward rather than reaching.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling is “a necessary component but not a sufficient one” and argues that it does not reach all aspects of intelligence.

r002.rationale: It calls scaling the strategy that works now, but does not cite other researchers’ pursuit of scaling as a pragmatic reason to pursue alternatives.

r003.rationale: It proposes building something “on top of” or “alongside” scaling, but does not advocate combining scaling resources such as GPUs or pretrained models with cognitive science or classical AI.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling is a powerful strategy, but we have to be clear about what we’re scaling and what we expect to get out of it. You can take a particular architecture, give it more data and more compute, and see substantial improvements. That’s an important empirical observation. But it doesn’t, by itself, tell us whether we have all the ingredients we need for intelligence.

One question I find useful is: what does the system have to figure out for itself, and what structure have we supplied? Even a system that looks like it’s learning everything from data has an architecture, an objective, and a process for selecting that data. There are assumptions built into all of those choices.

So I wouldn’t frame it as scaling versus finding better ideas. Better ideas can change what you get from scaling. The interesting question is whether a limitation is something that more computation will overcome, or whether you need to change the way the system represents and reasons about the problem. And distinguishing those possibilities is difficult—you need experiments that get at the underlying capability, rather than just an improvement in an aggregate score.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling improvements alone do not establish that all ingredients for intelligence are present, and some limits may require changing how systems represent and reason.

r002.rationale: It does not identify other researchers’ pursuit of scaling as a pragmatic reason to pursue alternatives.

r003.rationale: It does not advocate combining scaling resources such as GPUs or pretrained models with cognitive science or classical AI ideas.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling is clearly a powerful strategy. If you take a system and give it more compute, more data, and more capacity, you can get improvements that are quite surprising. But I’d separate that empirical observation from the stronger claim that scaling a particular architecture will give us everything we mean by intelligence.

The question for me is: what is the system learning, and what does that allow it to do? Predicting observations is useful, but we also want systems that can reason about interventions—what would happen if I did something differently—and construct explanations that we can inspect and criticize. Those capabilities might improve with scale, but we need to establish that rather than assume it.

So I don’t see scaling and developing better ideas as competing strategies. You want to scale, but you also want to understand which representations, objectives, and forms of computation are worth scaling. Otherwise, you can make enormous progress on a measurable task while leaving some of the underlying questions about intelligence unresolved.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes scaling’s empirical gains from the claim that scaling alone will deliver everything meant by intelligence, and says other ideas are also needed.

r002.rationale: It does not mention other researchers pursuing scaling or that this motivates pragmatic exploration of alternatives.

r003.rationale: It calls for better ideas alongside scaling, but does not identify cognitive science or classical AI ideas, or resources such as GPUs and pretrained models.
